phases.evidence: Repository metadata, public claims, examples, canonical CLI smoke checks, native execution of the Sotlas-written lexer subset, and an integrated Sotlas-written compiler frontend that rejects malformed input, unsupported aggregate members, invalid break/continue/return context, unresolved local names, and assignment to immutable locals with source locations, rejects duplicate top-level declarations, parameters, and same-block locals, and compiles a program with parameters and mutable locals to executable C.
phases.boundary: The native frontend is an experimental seven-module parser/emitter subset with limited lexical and structural semantic checks; global name resolution, full type checking, a complete semantic analyzer, and production replacement are not implemented, and it is not a stage1/stage2 fixed-point proof.

phases.evidence: Canonical check pipeline and typed AST semantic cases; undeclared names retain source locations and offer a close-name suggestion only when a visible symbol is a strong match.
phases.boundary: Most semantic cases are checker tests; native execution is limited to explicit fixtures.

phases.evidence: Canonical ownership/SIR placement, static rejection, legacy native probes, and production C11 execution of the supported region, direct, whisper, ISLAND-to-EXCLUSIVE handover, and repr(C) external-wrapper subsets. Native caller probes check destructor counts and transferred field values.
phases.boundary: The supported structured subset is tested; arbitrary CFG and full runtime ARC remain outside the contract.

phases.evidence: Canonical authority checks, typed SIR facts, and ABI contract validation.
phases.boundary: Reference ABI tests do not imply vendor GPU/NPU execution.

phases.evidence: Canonical state typing and transition validation.
phases.boundary: Only declared state-transition forms are accepted.

phases.evidence: Effect inference and backend rejection contracts.
phases.boundary: Effect checking does not sandbox external side effects.

phases.evidence: Canonical typed plans/SIR; the reference CPU runner interprets pure integer/boolean stages and schedules independent layers with error/cancellation propagation. C11 entrypoints execute pure scalar integer, f32/f64, and bool graphs in deterministic dependency order, including graphs with independent stages. C and Sotlas callers can invoke the generated entrypoint through its checked C ABI declaration; a companion ABI returns all stage outputs and checks caller pointers. Independent-stage outputs are compared with the reference runner, and `flow-run --backend c11` compiles, executes, and reports the outputs of a checked scalar plan.
phases.boundary: The reference interpreter and native backend cover different instruction/type subsets; native signed overflow is not defined by the language. C11 uses a serial fallback and does not promise parallel speedup. Source calls require the exact generated symbol and an @system function; there is no dedicated Flow invocation syntax. The all-outputs ABI has no structured native stage failure or cancellation channel. Ownership payloads and GPU/NPU dispatch remain unsupported.

phases.evidence: Target normalization, feature contracts, and LLVM emission checks.
phases.boundary: This is not a complete platform ABI or a Sotlas machine-code backend.

phases.evidence: Checked DEVICE lifecycle and reference provider failure contracts, plus an optional native OpenCL f32 vector-add dispatched by Sotlas-generated C11 code and verified with a C caller. A tested runtime policy selects CPU, requires OpenCL, or falls back to CPU when the runtime/GPU is unavailable and reports the chosen backend. GPU enumeration and index selection are tested. OpenCL event profiling separates input uploads, kernel execution, and readback. On Linux, a fault-injecting OpenCL provider exercises 12 initialization, dispatch, readback, and profiling failures without a physical GPU and aborts if any acquired handle leaks.
phases.boundary: OpenCL covers one explicit C ABI kernel; enumeration indices are not persistent hardware identifiers. The simulated provider validates host-side cleanup only and does not validate hardware behavior. Flow stages are not lowered to GPU; NPU, vendor-specific memory domains, async APIs, and full host-to-host benchmark reporting remain unavailable.

phases.evidence: Foreign boundary classification, explicit unsafe checks, and fail-closed validation.
phases.boundary: Trust labels do not create process isolation or a sandbox.

phases.evidence: Supported preconditions, refinements, and deterministic reports.
phases.boundary: Only the documented predicate subset is proved.

phases.evidence: Source and checked Flow call/dependency explanations.
phases.boundary: Ambiguous mutation and unresolved control flow remain fail-closed.

phases.evidence: Certified graph recovery and selected pure SIR equivalence cases.
phases.boundary: Proof is limited to the tested normalization and scalar subset.

phases.evidence: Effect policy checks and sequential compensation behavior.
phases.boundary: Parallel transactional execution and arbitrary rollback semantics are rejected.

phases.evidence: Selection among checked eligible Flow alternatives, fallback reports, and explicit provider availability requirements. Non-CPU execution requires a bound provider executor; executor results are checked against the selected stage set.
phases.boundary: Provider availability and executor bindings are supplied by the caller; there is no built-in Flow-to-GPU lowering or physical-device discovery.

phases.evidence: Canonical SIR facts, validation, and reports.
phases.boundary: SIR body lowering remains a certified subset, not complete lowering for the language.

phases.evidence: Direct LLVM subset emission and native execution, plus C11/LLVM differential checks for unsigned parameter/literal addition, subtraction, multiplication, defined wraparound, signed comparison inputs, and f32 multiplication and f64 addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and all six comparison predicates, including NaN behavior.
phases.boundary: Parity covers only tested forms. LLVM provides target code generation; Sotlas does not yet own register allocation or a machine backend.
Reports describe only facts represented by the checked subset.
